extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, and scholars interested in Margaret Mitchell's Gone with the Wind and literary/historical criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and evaluative points used in critical discussion of Gone with the Wind that readers and writers can use to judge or craft historical fiction (structure, genre, characterization, historical research, representation, reception, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Readability / narrative clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel is known for its exceptional 'readability.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitchell used a smooth linear narrative structure and arranged the novel chronologically, which contributes to readability. Evaluate whether prose, pacing, and narrative flow make the work easy and compelling to read.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronological structure / bildungsroman form
rubrics_metrics.description: Margaret Mitchell arranged Gone with the Wind chronologically, focusing on the life and experiences of the main character, Scarlett O'Hara, as she grew from adolescence into adulthood. This is a type of Bildungsroman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the chronological ordering and coming-of-age focus convincingly show moral and psychological growth (Scarlett ages from 16 to 28 across 1861–1873). For writers: using a clear temporal arc and tracking protagonist development supports a bildungsroman.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre fit: historical romance vs historical novel
rubrics_metrics.description: Gone with the Wind is often placed in the literary subgenre of the historical romance novel; Pamela Regis has argued it is more appropriately classified as a historical novel, as it does not contain all elements of the romance genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the work contains the formal and thematic elements of the chosen subgenre. Consider whether romantic plotlines dominate or whether broader historical depiction and social commentary reclassify it as historical fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and significance of the title / intertextuality
rubrics_metrics.description: The title is from a line of Ernest Dowson's poem and, in a general sense, is a metaphor for the demise of a way of life in the South before the Civil War; when taken in context it also alludes to erotic loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how effectively a title functions as metaphor and whether intertextual references deepen thematic resonance. For writers: choose titles that encapsulate central themes or motifs and consider intertextual layers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical research and fact-checking
rubrics_metrics.description: Mitchell worked for six months checking the historical references and rewriting early chapters before publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate accuracy, plausibility, and the richness of historical detail. For authors of historical fiction: thorough checking of historical references and revision (including reworking openings) improves credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization and vivid supporting cast
rubrics_metrics.description: The plot is rich with vivid characters (detailed main and secondary characters such as Scarlett, Rhett, Ashley, Melanie, Mammy, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge depth, complexity, and distinctiveness of main and secondary characters, their growth or stasis, and how they serve the novel's themes. Strong characterization includes memorable traits, believable motivations, and interpersonal dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of slavery and race — representation ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Slavery in Gone with the Wind is a backdrop to a story that is essentially about other things; plantation fiction from this tradition is written from the perspective and values of an enslaver and tends to present slaves as docile and happy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critically evaluate depiction of enslaved people, whether the portrayal romanticizes or flattens Black characters, and the ethical implications. For writers: be mindful of perspective, power dynamics, and the risk of perpetuating harmful stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caste/class depiction and social hierarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters are organized into two basic groups along class lines: the white planter class and the black house servant class; house servants are presented as the highest 'caste' of enslaved people in Mitchell's system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how class and caste are constructed and whether social hierarchies are interrogated or reproduced. Examine narrative choices that privilege particular viewpoints or normalize inequitable social structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archetypal roles (e.g., Southern belle, mammy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel employs archetypes such as the 'southern belle' and the 'mammy' (Mammy never considers life away from Tara; the southern belle is an archetype of antebellum upper-class young women).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate usage of archetypes: do they illuminate themes or reduce characters to stereotypes? Consider whether the narrative problematizes or reinforces archetypal roles and their cultural meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portrayal of women's experience and agency
rubrics_metrics.description: Gone with the Wind features a coming-of-age story of Scarlett O'Hara, whose moral and psychological growth and survival strategies (running mills, managing a store, marrying for money) are central.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how female agency is depicted in relation to social constraints, survival, and moral complexity. For writers: depict realistic motivations, contradictions, and resourcefulness in women's choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and sexual content (erotic elements)
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel has been described as an early classic of the erotic historical genre because it is thought to contain some degree of pornography.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the explicitness and function of sexual content: does it serve character development or titillation? Evaluate whether erotic elements align with genre expectations and thematic aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and epic scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the novel is more than 1,000 pages long, the plot is rich with vivid characters and spans a broad historical period and many events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the length and scope are justified by narrative complexity and thematic range. For writers: maintain narrative momentum and avoid superfluous material in epic-length works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural reception and lasting influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Gone with the Wind was popular from the outset, became a bestseller, received the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction, was adapted into a highly successful 1939 film, and has been absorbed into American popular culture; it is also a controversial reference point for subsequent writers of the South.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both contemporary and retrospective reception, awards, adaptations, and cultural impact. Consider how later critiques (e.g., about race) change the work's standing over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing, authorship process, and narrative planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Mitchell wrote the book's final moments first and then wrote the events that led to them; she and her husband edited the final version together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For practitioners: consider planning the ending to guide plotting, and the value of collaborative editing. Evaluate whether editorial choices (structure, pacing, chapter openings) strengthen the narrative.
